In these studies, although environmental firms contribute to pol- lution abatement, they cause distortions due to imperfect competition. This paper analyzes non-cooperative environmental policies in the presence of imperfectly competitive environmental industries and transboundary pollution across countries (e.g., greenhouse gases, acid rains, and pollution of shared water resources). The importance of analyzing non-cooperative policymaking under trans- boundary pollution is illustrated by the issue of global climate change. As King and van den Bergh (2021) and others have pointed out, the current initiatives on this issue are a correction of unilateral domestic actions. Under the Paris Agreement, participant countries are supposed to commit themselves to Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) for environmental protection. In addition to taxes or other emission pricing measures, subsidies are important environmental policy instruments.4 When pollution exter - nalities and imperfect competition exist, efficient policy instruments consist of taxes on polluting firms and subsidies to environmental firms (see David and Sinclair- Desgagn 2010); while taxes correct pollution externalities, subsidies remove the distortion of imperfect competition.5 This paper examines how transboundary pollu- tion distorts these policy choices.

In this the paper, starting from Breton and Sbragia (2019), Baris and Zaccour (2018) and Masoudi and Zaccour (2018), we propose a two-stage coalition forma- tion game, where in the first stage countries decide whether or not to sign the agree- ment and in the second stage, signatories and defectors select their levels of miti- gation and adaptation in order to minimize their cost function. nodes.answer: Despite some improvements in financial flows after the Paris Agreement, fossil fuel investments remain widespread and the growth in clean energy investments is minimal.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Achieving a clean energy transition requires global financial flows to be redirected away from fossil fuels and into renewable energy. While capital market actors and multilateral financial institutions have been the subject of significant scholarly attention, public bilat - eral financial institutions, especially Export Credit Agencies (ECAs), have been largely overlooked. This is an important oversight given ECAs are the source of billions of dollars of public finance for fossil fuels, which has helped to lock-in recipient countries to fossil fuel energy systems. Using a panel dataset of ECA transactions in the energy sector, we show that despite some improvements in financial flows after the Paris Agreement in 2015, fossil fuel investments remain pervasive and growth in clean energy investments is mini - mal. To better understand changes in ECA portfolios, we examine the cases of the Export- Import Bank of the United States (Exlm) and UK Export Finance (UKEF). Drawing on elite interviews, we identify three factors that are shaping Exlm S and UKEF S capacity to promote renewable energy exports: the extent of political control over the bureaucracy, the size and composition of green industrial bases, and the policy tools available to both ECAs to support the renewables sector.

nodes.paragraph: 2018 ). While capital market actors and multilateral financial institutions have been the subject of significant scholarly attention (Kim and Lee 2021 ; Stoll et al. 2021 ; Ameli et al. 2020 ), public bilateral financial institutions, especially Export Credit Agencies (ECAs), have been largely overlooked (Peterson and Downie 2023 ; Klasen et al. 2022 This is an important oversight given that ECAs are the largest source of bilateral public finance for fossil fuels, which has helped to lock-in recipient countries to fossil fuel energy systems, such as coal fired power stations in Asia and gas infrastructure in Africa (O Manique et al. 2024 ; Chen et al. 2021 ). At the same time, as institutions under the control of national governments, ECAs, unlike private capital or multilateral financial institutions, should be well placed to respond to national climate policy objectives, and use their financial instruments, such as risk insur - ance, to crowd-in private investment for clean energy projects. In this context, it is no surprise that ECAs are facing growing international pressure to align their activities with the goals of the Paris Agreement.

nodes.question: What percentage of city Climate Action Plans (CAPs) globally fail to set sufficient decarbonization pledges?
nodes.answer: Over half of city CAPs globally fail to set sufficient decarbonization pledges.
nodes.paragraph: Conventional practice sees cities focusing on reducing emissions from specific domains under their jurisdictional authority, including transportation, waste management, and municipal facilities. Cities have the power to act on other domains such as land use and development, however they often struggle to coordinate climate action through these tools and decision-makers may lack understanding of the scien - tific connections between policy tools and climate (Tang et al. 2010 ; Bierbaum et al. 2012 ). Given limitations to city powers in many contexts, it is not surprising that past research has questioned the ambitions of U.S. cities, documenting insufficient emissions reduction targets (Boswell et al. 2010 ). Further, research on CAPs globally has found that over half of city CAPs fail to set sufficient decarbonization pledges, and evidence-based climate action planning is not prevalent enough (Aboagye and Sharifi 2023 ). As such, there are growing 1 3 61 Climatic Change (2025) 178:61 concerns about whether U.S. cities can or will meaningfully mitigate climate change at the level demanded by the climate crisis (Deetjan et al. 2018 ; Meerow and Woodruff 2020 ).

nodes.question: What kind of commitments have governments made regarding GHG emissions in recent years?
nodes.answer: Many governments have made significant commitments to reduce GHG emissions both individually and in coordination with others.
nodes.paragraph: Emissions from fossil fuels started before the Industrial Era and became the dominant source of anthropogenic emission to the atmosphere from around 1950 with their relative share continuing to increase until the present. The Kyoto Protocol,an environmental agreement adopted in 1997 by many of the parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) is working towards B Pilar Poncela pilar.poncela@uam.es Department of Economic Analysis: Quantitative Economics, Universidad Aut noma de Madrid,Madrid, Spain 2Department of Statistics, Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Getafe, Spain 123 1380 A. de Juan et al. curbing CO 2emissions globally. In recent years, many Governments have made very signi cant commitments as regards the reduction of GHG emissions both in coor- dination with others and individually. Among these initiatives is the Paris Agreementof 2015. The aim of this agreement is to keep the increase in global temperature this century below 2 C. For this purpose, the various signatory countries have adopted commitments to reduce their emissions. In the case of the European Union (EU), the coordination of actions to mitigate the effects of climate change and to promote the green transition has mainly been based on the European Green Deal.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|International climate agreements|Nationally determined contributions (ndcs)_qna_028
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What are some of the key components of Spain's climate strategy mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Key components of Spain's climate strategy include the Climate Change and Energy Transition Law, the National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) 2021-2030, the National Plan for Adapting to Climate Change (PNACC), and the Just Transition Strategy.
nodes.paragraph: Notable among such actions is the EuropeanClimate Law, enacted in June 2021, which sets a legally binding target of net zero GHG emissions by 2050 and requires both Member States and EU institutions to take the necessary measures to meet this target. This Law also sets an intermediatetarget for 2030 of reducing GHG emissions in the EU as a whole by 55% (from 1990 levels). The success of these agreements critically hinges on the implementation of effective policies at the national level. In this paper, we focus on a particular countrywithin the EU, namely, Spain, in which the basic pillars of such a strategy are the Climate Change and Energy Transition Law, the National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) 2021 2030, the National Plan for Adapting to Climate Change (PNACC by its Spanish abbreviation) and the Just Transition Strategy; see Banco de Espa a (2021 ). For example, within the framework of the Law on Climate Change and Energy Transition, proposals have been made for notable changes to patterns of mobility and the creation of low-emission zones in major cities.
